candidates.quote: The Way is like a wide road. It is not at all difficult to find. The trouble with people is simply that they do not look for it. You go home and look for it and there will be teachers enough for you.
candidates.author: Mencius
candidates.locator: Book VI, Part B, 2 (Mencius answering Ts’ao Chiao); Penguin Classics, 1970, the section opening at p. 172
candidates.whyThisMonth: It puts the Way within reach of whoever is awake this early: the road is wide and close to home, and the only failure it names is not looking for it.

candidates.quote: To study the buddha way is to study the self. To study the self is to forget the self. To forget the self is to be actualized by myriad things. When actualized by myriad things, your body and mind as well as the bodies and minds of others drop away.
candidates.author: Dōgen
candidates.locator: section 4, in Moon in a Dewdrop: Writings of Zen Master Dōgen, ed. Kazuaki Tanahashi (North Point Press, 1985), p. 70; the essay opens at p. 69
candidates.whyThisMonth: It says the Way begins with the self a person wakes up as and then leads straight out of it, which is renewal without any need to arrive anywhere.

candidates.quote: I put one foot forward and drew the other back. If in the morning I had a genuine longing to seek eternal life, by the evening the attack of a whole host of desires had reduced it to impotence. Worldly desires were striving to keep me by their chains just where I was, while the voice of faith was calling, ‘To the road! to the road! What is left of life is but little and the journey before you is long.’
candidates.author: Al-Ghazali
candidates.work: Deliverance from Error, in The Faith and Practice of al-Ghazali
candidates.locator: section III, The Classes of Seekers (the way of the mystics), pp. 56 to 57 (George Allen and Unwin, 1953); the inner speech runs on for three more sentences in Watt, and the card closes it at long
candidates.whyThisMonth: Everyone who has meant to begin and then not begun knows the one foot forward and the other drawn back, and this is the only answer that has ever worked on it.

candidates.quote: Wherefore my counsel is, that we hold fast ever to the heavenly way and follow after justice and virtue always, considering that the soul is immortal and able to endure every sort of good and every sort of evil. Thus shall we live dear to one another and to the gods, both while remaining here and when, like conquerors in the games who go round to gather gifts, we receive our reward. And it shall be well with us both in this life and in the pilgrimage of a thousand years which we have been describing.
candidates.author: Plato
candidates.locator: Book X, 621c to d, the closing sentences of the dialogue; Project Gutenberg ebook 1497, which prints a revised Jowett text
candidates.whyThisMonth: The longest argument in Western philosophy ends by telling the reader to keep to the road and promising that it will be well with them on it, which is the whole month in three sentences.
candidates.speaker: Socrates

candidates.quote: If the way which I have pointed out as leading to this result seems exceedingly hard, it may nevertheless be discovered. Needs must it be hard, since it is so seldom found. How would it be possible, if salvation were ready to our hand, and could without great labour be found, that it should be by almost all men neglected? But all things excellent are as difficult as they are rare.
candidates.author: Baruch Spinoza
candidates.locator: Part V, Proposition XLII, Note, the closing sentences of the work; Project Gutenberg ebook 3800
candidates.whyThisMonth: It admits at the end of a geometry of the soul that the way is hard, and then refuses to let that be a reason to leave it, which is what a hard morning needs said.

candidates.quote: Travel is in my opinion a very profitable exercise; the soul is there continually employed in observing new and unknown things, and I do not know, as I have often said a better school wherein to model life than by incessantly exposing to it the diversity of so many other lives, fancies, and usances, and by making it relish a perpetual variety of forms of human nature.
candidates.author: Michel de Montaigne
candidates.locator: Book III, ch. 9, Of Vanity (ed. W. Carew Hazlitt, 1877); Project Gutenberg ebook 3600; the sentence opens Besides these reasons, which the card drops, so the capital T is the card’s
candidates.whyThisMonth: It is the month’s claim that the road teaches, argued by a man who thought the school of other lives better than any other school.
candidates.translator: Charles Cotton, 1685 to 1686, revised by W. Carew Hazlitt, 1877

candidates.quote: Above all, do not lose your desire to walk: every day I walk myself into a state of well-being and walk away from every illness; I have walked myself into my best thoughts, and I know of no thought so burdensome that one cannot walk away from it.
candidates.author: Søren Kierkegaard
candidates.locator: Letter 150, to Henriette Kierkegaard, 1847 (Princeton University Press, 1978); the editor’s introduction to the same volume prints a semicolon where the letter prints a colon
candidates.whyThisMonth: It is the plainest prescription in philosophy, and it can be filled before breakfast: get up and walk, and the thought that seemed immovable moves.

candidates.quote: The Tao is in the Passage rather than the Path. It is the spirit of Cosmic Change,—the eternal growth which returns upon itself to produce new forms. It recoils upon itself like the dragon, the beloved symbol of the Taoists. It folds and unfolds as do the clouds.
candidates.author: Okakura Kakuzō
candidates.locator: ch. III, Taoism and Zennism (Fox, Duffield and Company, 1906); Project Gutenberg ebook 769
candidates.whyThisMonth: It is the month’s two words joined in one sentence: the way is the passing along it, and what that passing does is grow new forms out of the old.

candidates.quote: Life is occupied in both perpetuating itself and in surpassing itself; if all it does is maintain itself, then living is only not dying, and human existence is indistinguishable from an absurd vegetation; a life justifies itself only if its effort to perpetuate itself is integrated into its surpassing and if this surpassing has no other limits than those which the subject assigns himself.
candidates.author: Simone de Beauvoir
candidates.locator: Part III, the section on freedom and liberation, pp. 81 to 82 (Philosophical Library, 1948)
candidates.whyThisMonth: In the month of things starting to grow it draws the line between merely keeping going and going somewhere, and leaves the second within the reader’s gift.

candidates.quote: Travellers who require that every nation should resemble their native country, had better stay at home.
candidates.author: Mary Wollstonecraft
candidates.work: Letters Written During a Short Residence in Sweden, Norway, and Denmark
candidates.locator: Letter V (J. Johnson, 1796); Project Gutenberg ebook 3529, which prints the Cassell’s National Library text of 1889
candidates.whyThisMonth: It names the one condition on which travel teaches anything: that the traveller came to meet a place rather than to grade it.

candidates.quote: Those who contemplate the beauty of the earth find reserves of strength that will endure as long as life lasts. There is symbolic as well as actual beauty in the migration of the birds, the ebb and flow of the tides, the folded bud ready for the spring. There is something infinitely healing in the repeated refrains of nature—the assurance that dawn comes after night, and spring after the winter.
candidates.author: Rachel Carson
candidates.locator: the closing pages (Harper and Row, 1965); first printed as Help Your Child to Wonder, Woman’s Home Companion, July 1956
candidates.whyThisMonth: It is the April promise stated as a fact of nature rather than a hope, and it is read best at the hour when the dawn it names is actually arriving.

candidates.quote: Often the mountain gives itself most completely when I have no destination, when I reach nowhere in particular, but have gone out merely to be with the mountain as one visits a friend with no intention but to be with him.
candidates.author: Nan Shepherd
candidates.locator: p. 15 of the Canongate edition of 2011; first published by Aberdeen University Press, 1977; the sentence opens with Yet, which the card drops, so the capital O is the card’s
candidates.whyThisMonth: It is the anti-summit sentence: the way gives most on the days a person sets out with no errand, which is the freest thing a morning can be told.

candidates.quote: Patience, patience, patience, is what the sea teaches. Patience and faith. One should lie empty, open, choiceless as a beach—waiting for a gift from the sea.
candidates.author: Anne Morrow Lindbergh
candidates.locator: ch. 1, The Beach (Pantheon, 1955); the sentences follow The sea does not reward those who are too anxious, too greedy, or too impatient
candidates.whyThisMonth: It is the other half of the month: not the road walked but the road waited on, and it gives a reader something to do on a morning when nothing is moving.

candidates.quote: To awaken quite alone in a strange town is one of the pleasantest sensations in the world. You are surrounded by adventure. You have no idea of what is in store for you, but you will, if you are wise and know the art of travel, let yourself go on the stream of the unknown and accept whatever comes in the spirit in which the gods may offer it.
candidates.author: Freya Stark
candidates.locator: In the Moslem Quarter, the opening sentences of the chapter, p. 17 (John Murray, 1937); first collected in Baghdad, 1932
candidates.whyThisMonth: It is a waking sentence for the hour a reader is actually waking in, and it treats the unknown day ahead as the best thing about it.

candidates.quote: A subject to which few intellectuals ever give a thought is the right to be a vagrant, the freedom to wander. Yet vagrancy is deliverance, and life on the open road is the essence of freedom. To have the courage to smash the chains with which modern life has weighted us (under the pretext that it was giving us more liberty), then to take up the symbolic stick and bundle, and get out!
candidates.author: Isabelle Eberhardt
candidates.work: Pencilled Notes, in The Oblivion Seekers and Other Writings
candidates.locator: p. 68 (City Lights Books, 1975); the French is the piece on vagabondage collected posthumously in Pages d’Islam, ed. Victor Barrucand
candidates.whyThisMonth: It is the month’s setting out at its most unreasonable and most alive, written by someone who did it, and it ends on the one verb the reader can use.

candidates.quote: When the spirit swells my breast I love to roam leisurely among the green hills; or sometimes, sitting on the brink of the murmuring Missouri, I marvel at the great blue overhead.
candidates.author: Zitkala-Ša
candidates.work: The Great Spirit, in American Indian Stories
candidates.locator: the opening sentence of the essay (Hayworth Publishing House, 1921); first printed as Why I Am a Pagan, The Atlantic Monthly, December 1902; Project Gutenberg ebook 10376
candidates.whyThisMonth: It is a spring walk taken for no reason but gladness, and it puts a reader outdoors and looking up before the day has asked anything of them.
